title: One governed order pipeline must pass every gate—not five isolated demos
goal: Consolidate ingestion rescue, array expansion, join planning, masking, and workload identity into one auditable Databricks/Snowflake delivery path.
concept:
A restaurant does not call dinner successful because the ingredients arrived. The order must pass receiving, preparation, assembly, privacy, and delivery.

Our synthetic order pipeline has the same chain: a secretless EKS workload authenticates; malformed rows remain inspectable; valid orders expand into item rows; a small product lookup enriches them; customer email is masked for analysts. Every gate must preserve evidence for the next one.
example: File orders-50.json contains order o-50 with two items and one malformed record. The pipeline should publish two enriched item rows, retain one error record, and show ***@example.com to the analyst. A valid identity without table grants must still stop before ingestion.

use_case.when: Use an end-to-end consolidation case when individual features work but you need evidence that their boundaries compose safely.
use_case.example: An EKS order service loads semi-structured files, preserves errors, explodes items, enriches from a 12 MB product table, and publishes an analyst-safe view.
use_case.decision: Run the smallest representative case that crosses identity, data quality, transformation, performance, and governance. A unit demo is simpler when only one boundary changed.

practice: Toggle identity, malformed-row handling, lookup size, and analyst role. Predict the first failed gate and the surviving evidence.
boundary: The local Python and JavaScript models use three synthetic rows and arithmetic rules. They do not execute Databricks or Snowflake SQL, verify tokens, reproduce optimizer plans, catalog privileges, copy history, costs, cloud storage, encryption, concurrency, lineage, or recovery behavior.

title: request(10) grants ten signals—it does not create ten storage slots
goal: Separate reactive-stream demand from publisher buffer capacity.
concept:
A deli ticket says the counter may hand you ten sandwiches. It does not say your bag can hold ten.

In Java Flow, Subscription.request(n) adds demand: the publisher must not send more onNext signals than requested. Buffer capacity is a separate implementation resource. Safe systems bound both outstanding demand and queued items.
example: A subscriber requests 10 records but processes 3 per tick. With a publisher buffer of 4, a burst can fill the queue before all ten requested records are delivered. Replenishing demand only after processing keeps the outstanding window bounded.

use_case.when: Use bounded demand when a Java subscriber consumes events slower than a producer can offer them.
use_case.example: A Kafka-adjacent enrichment stage asks for four records, processes two, then asks for two more.
use_case.decision: Choose a demand window from downstream capacity and latency. Configure publisher buffers separately; use a simple blocking queue when a full reactive protocol adds no value.

practice: Change demand, buffer capacity, and processing rate. Predict delivered, queued, and rejected items.
boundary: The Java trace is synchronous arithmetic, not a real Publisher. It omits threading, SubmissionPublisher lag/drop handlers, reentrant requests, cancellation, errors, multiple subscribers, memory visibility, and Reactive Streams rule verification.

Demand for up to ten signals, not ten buffer slots

title: A pilot that avoids the hard case proves only the easy case
goal: Select a low-blast-radius pilot that still exercises the majority of in-scope capabilities.
concept:
A driving test held only in an empty parking lot is safe, but it does not prove motorway readiness.

A good platform pilot balances two dimensions: failure must be affordable, and the workload must still exercise representative risks. Predefine measurable success and the next decision. Recommendations and redesign findings are useful evidence, not pilot failure.
example: Three pipeline candidates exist. A tiny CSV batch is safe but exercises 2 of 7 required capabilities. A payments stream exercises all 7 but has unacceptable blast radius. A duplicated order stream exercises 6 of 7 with synthetic customer data and reversible cutover. The third is the decision-grade pilot.

use_case.when: Use this method before declaring a platform pattern ready for a broader migration wave.
use_case.example: Choose a shadow order pipeline that includes schema drift, backfill, observability, privacy, and rollback without serving production decisions.
use_case.decision: Prefer low criticality plus high scope coverage. If no candidate has both, create a shadow or replay environment rather than selecting an easy but unrepresentative demo.

practice: Score three candidates for risk, scope coverage, and evidence quality; move the threshold and observe the choice.
boundary: The weighted score is a decision aid, not an AWS formula. It omits political sponsorship, opportunity cost, regulatory approval, team skill, dependency timing, and qualitative failure modes.

title: Route on MCP headers—then reject a body that disagrees
goal: Use MCP 2026 header-based routing without letting a proxy and server interpret different requests.
concept:
An envelope label helps the mailroom route a package, but the label and form inside must describe the same destination.

For MCP 2026-07-28 Streamable HTTP, Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name support routing before parsing the full JSON-RPC body. The server must reject a mismatch with MCP error -32020. The headers are duplicated routing metadata, not a second source of truth.
example: A gateway routes Mcp-Method: tools/call and Mcp-Name: query_orders to the data-tool pool. If the body says tools/call for delete_catalog, the server rejects it instead of executing either interpretation.

use_case.when: Use header routing when an MCP gateway, WAF, or load balancer must steer requests before decoding the JSON-RPC body.
use_case.example: Send query tools to a read-only pool and image tools to a GPU pool, then verify header/body equality at the server boundary.
use_case.decision: Use the headers for early routing only on the 2026-07-28 protocol path. Keep body parsing and mismatch rejection authoritative; older protocol versions need their documented transport behavior.

practice: Change method or name in one layer. Predict the route and the server result.
boundary: The model compares strings only. It omits HTTP parsing, protocol negotiation, Mcp-Param headers, proxies, signatures, authorization, JSON-RPC batch behavior, redirects, CORS, request smuggling, and SDK interoperability.

title: An AI copilot can suggest where to edit a structure—the engineer still chooses the change
goal: Understand a new human-in-the-loop topology-optimization result without turning its synthetic preference model into a production claim.
concept:
Imagine editing a bridge-shaped puzzle. Instead of clicking many candidate regions, an assistant highlights the long member or complex junction most likely to need attention.

A new Communications Engineering paper frames region selection as image segmentation with a U-Net. It trains on synthetic preference masks for the longest member or most complex connection, then recommends plausible edit regions inside a topology-optimization loop. The human still selects and modifies the design.
example: The paper reports demonstration cases improving manufacturability or linear buckling load by 39% with 15 seconds added versus a simplified baseline. Those numbers belong to the reported cases, not a general guarantee. The browser ranks invented regions only; it does not solve mechanics.

use_case.when: Study this work when interactive structural optimization is bottlenecked by repeated manual region selection.
use_case.example: A structural engineer asks the copilot to highlight a long slender member, then decides whether to thicken, remove, or constrain it before rerunning optimization.
use_case.decision: Treat it as an accepted peer-reviewed research workflow. Require physical constraints, expert studies, compute cost, uncertainty, manufacturability, and validation on your geometry before engineering use.

practice: Change the synthetic preference from longest member to complex junction. Predict which invented region is highlighted.
boundary: The model uses three invented scores. It does not run U-Net inference, topology optimization, finite elements, buckling analysis, skeletonization, manufacturing constraints, uncertainty, or the paper's datasets. Reported 39% and 15-second figures are case results, not reproduced here.

title: GITHUB_OUTPUT writes strings; fromJSON restores the type
goal: Convert step-output text before using it as a boolean, number, object, or matrix.
concept:
A shipping label that says 10 is text until a system parses it as a number.

GitHub step outputs are strings. Expressions can coerce some values, but explicit fromJSON() makes the intended type visible and supports objects, arrays, booleans, and numbers. Invalid JSON should fail rather than quietly become policy.
example: A planning step writes timeout=10 and experimental=false to GITHUB_OUTPUT. The consumer uses fromJSON for timeout-minutes and continue-on-error. The string false must not be treated as a nonempty truthy value by surrounding shell or application logic.

use_case.when: Use fromJSON when a job or step output represents a number, boolean, array, object, or dynamic matrix.
use_case.example: A planner emits a JSON matrix and a numeric timeout for downstream test jobs.
use_case.decision: Keep plain strings as strings. Parse typed control data exactly once at the workflow boundary and validate the producer's JSON.

practice: Toggle raw values and parsing. Predict the resulting type and gate decision.
boundary: The browser uses JavaScript JSON.parse, which illustrates JSON typing but is not GitHub's full expression evaluator. It omits YAML parsing, loose equality, NaN rules, secrets, output limits, multiline values, and runner execution.

title: 103 can start preload—it is not the final response
goal: Use HTTP 103 Early Hints as speculative performance metadata without treating it as success.
concept:
A restaurant can tell you the bread is coming while the kitchen still decides whether the main dish is available.

HTTP 103 is an informational response. It can carry likely Link: rel=preload fields so a client starts fetching resources while the origin computes the final response. The client must still wait for and process the final status and headers independently.
example: An API-backed page sends 103 for /app.css at 20 ms, then discovers at 180 ms that the user is unauthorized and sends final 401. The stylesheet preload may have started; the application must not render authenticated content or mark the request successful.

use_case.when: Use 103 when final response generation is slow but useful preload links are known early and clients/intermediaries handle informational responses correctly.
use_case.example: A gateway emits a stylesheet preload while an upstream page request waits on a regional database.
use_case.decision: Measure actual latency benefit and client support. Skip 103 when the final headers arrive quickly, hints are unstable or sensitive, or HTTP/1.1 compatibility is uncertain.

practice: Change final status and hint timing. Predict what may start early and what remains undecided.
boundary: The model uses a simple timeline. It does not open HTTP connections, implement caching, browser preload rules, HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 framing, intermediary behavior, credential modes, content policy, or the RFC's cross-origin security considerations.
